lesson.subtitle: Lesson 1 -- The Two-Minute Version of You
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Flavio Gattaz | Lesson 1 -- The Two-Minute Version of You

listenings.text: All right, my turn. I run a construction company in Denver. It is a family-run business, about sixty people on the payroll, and my grandfather started it in 1974, so I am the third generation. We build schools and clinics, mostly public work, and at the moment we have five projects open at the same time, which is two more than I would like. My background is civil engineering, and I will be honest with you, nobody has asked me to design anything in eleven years. What I actually do is people, money and clients, in that order. And that is why I am in this room. I learned to run a company by running it, which sounds fine until you realize it means you have never once seen how anybody else does it. So I am here to find out what I have been getting wrong.

People ask me what we listen for in the first two minutes, and the honest answer is that we listen for whether you have thought about the question. Most candidates recite the resume in order. They start with the degree, they walk through every job, and they arrive at the present tense about ninety seconds in. That is the one part of the conversation we did not need, because we can read all of it on the form. A good opening is three things. What you run, how big it is in one number, and what you are working on right now that you did not have to take on. That last one tells me more than the whole employment history, because it is the only part that was a choice. And before somebody asks, no, I do not care about perfect English. I care whether you can keep a conversation going. A slow, clear answer beats a fast, unclear one every single time, and everybody on this side of the table already knows that.

Family firms make up around two thirds of all companies in the world, and that figure is quoted so often that people stop hearing what it hides, which is how few of them ever get past the second generation. The reason is not usually money. The reason is that the person who inherits the company inherits the technical job as well, and nobody sits them down and teaches them the other half. You take over as the engineer, or as the baker, or as the one who knows the machines, and then one Monday you are also the one deciding who gets hired and what the company is going to be in five years. We spoke to a dozen owners in that position for this series. Almost all of them said the same thing about going back to study. They tend to go back late, in their forties, and they do it because they can already see the ceiling they are about to hit.
